subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: In the Word-RAM model used for running-time analysis, the word size w (in bits) for an input of size n is assumed to satisfy which bound?
options: w = 1 bit, so every operation is a bit operation
w = n bits, so any input value fits in one word
w is unbounded, so any integer arithmetic is O(1)
log n ≤ w ≤ c·log n for some constant c ≥ 1
explanation: Words must be at least log n bits so an index into n memory cells fits in one word, and at most c·log n bits so huge numbers cannot be packed into one word for free. An unbounded word would make, for example, adding two Θ(n)-bit Fibonacci numbers look O(1), which is the tempting but wrong unit-cost assumption.
concept: Word-RAM: unit-cost operations on words of Θ(log n) bits.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Which statement is the definition of T(n) = O(f(n))?
options: There exist constants c > 0 and n₀ ≥ 0 such that T(n) ≥ c·f(n) for all n ≥ n₀
There exist constants c > 0 and n₀ ≥ 0 such that T(n) ≤ c·f(n) for all n ≥ n₀
T(n) ≤ f(n) for every n ≥ 1
T(n)/f(n) tends to 0 as n tends to infinity
explanation: Big-O is an upper bound up to a constant factor, required only beyond some threshold n₀. The '≥' version defines Ω, and the limit-to-zero version defines the stricter little-o, so neither is the definition of O.
concept: O = asymptotic upper bound with explicit c and n₀.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: What is the best-case running time of insertion sort on n elements, and on which input does it occur?
options: Θ(n log n), when the input is already sorted
Θ(n), when the input is sorted in reverse
Θ(n), when the input is already sorted
Θ(n²), on every input
explanation: On sorted input the inner while-test fails immediately for each key, so each of the n − 1 iterations costs O(1), giving Θ(n). Reverse-sorted input is the worst case (Θ(n²)), and Θ(n²) on every input describes selection sort, not insertion sort.
concept: Insertion sort is adaptive: Θ(n + I) where I = number of inversions.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Using the master theorem, solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n).
options: Θ(n log n)
Θ(n)
Θ(n²)
Θ(log n)
explanation: Here a = 2, b = 2, d = 1, so log_b a = 1 = d: the balanced case, giving Θ(n^d log n) = Θ(n log n). Answering Θ(n) ignores that every one of the log n levels of the recursion tree does Θ(n) work.
concept: a = b^d ⇒ Θ(n^d log n).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Binary search on a sorted array of n elements has which worst-case running time, and what is its precondition?
options: Θ(log n); the array must already be sorted
Θ(log n); the array may be in any order
Θ(n); the array must already be sorted
Θ(1); the array must contain distinct keys
explanation: Each probe halves the search interval, so the worst case (key absent) takes about ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 probes. The correctness argument that discards one half depends entirely on sortedness, so running it on unsorted data gives wrong answers.
concept: T(n) = T(n/2) + c ⇒ Θ(log n); needs sorted input.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: If every strongly connected component of a directed graph G is contracted to a single node, what kind of graph results?
options: Always a directed acyclic graph (DAG)
Always a directed cycle
Always a rooted tree
A DAG only when G itself is acyclic
explanation: If the component graph had a cycle, every vertex in the SCCs on that cycle would be mutually reachable, so those SCCs would merge into one, contradicting maximality. Hence the component graph is a DAG for every G, not only when G is acyclic.
concept: The SCC component graph G^SCC is always a DAG.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: A minimum spanning tree of a connected undirected graph with V vertices and E edges contains how many edges?
options: V
E − V + 1
explanation: Any spanning tree is connected and acyclic on all V vertices, which forces exactly V − 1 edges. E − V + 1 is the number of edges left out of the tree (the cyclomatic number), a common mix-up.
concept: Every spanning tree has exactly V − 1 edges.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Which condition on edge weights is required for Dijkstra's algorithm to be guaranteed correct?
options: The graph has no negative-weight cycle (negative edges are allowed)
All edge weights are distinct
All edge weights are non-negative
The graph is undirected
explanation: Dijkstra finalises the closest unfinalised vertex, which is safe only if no later edge can lower an already-minimum distance, i.e. w ≥ 0. Merely having no negative cycle is the condition for Bellman–Ford; Dijkstra can still fail with a single negative edge.
concept: Dijkstra needs w(e) ≥ 0; negative edges need Bellman–Ford.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Which pair of properties indicates that dynamic programming is an appropriate technique for a problem?
options: Optimal substructure and the greedy-choice property
Disjoint subproblems and a linear-time combine step
A canonical input and a sorted output
Optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems
explanation: DP pays off when optimal solutions are built from optimal sub-solutions and the same subproblems recur, so tabulating them avoids recomputation. The greedy-choice property is what lets greedy skip all but one subproblem; disjoint subproblems characterise divide and conquer.
concept: DP = optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: For selecting the maximum number of mutually compatible tasks (activity/task selection), the provably optimal greedy rule picks the next task by:
options: Earliest start time
Earliest finish time
Shortest duration
Fewest conflicts with other tasks
explanation: Choosing the earliest-finishing compatible task leaves the most room for the rest, and the 'greedy stays ahead' argument proves it optimal. Earliest start fails on one long early task, and shortest duration fails when a short task overlaps two compatible longer ones.
concept: Task selection: sort by finish time; proof by greedy stays ahead.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: The 0/1 knapsack DP runs in O(nW) time for n items and capacity W. Why is this called pseudo-polynomial?
options: It is polynomial only when the item weights are distinct
It uses O(nW) space, which is not polynomial
It is polynomial on average but exponential in the worst case
It is polynomial in the numeric value W but exponential in the number of bits needed to write W
explanation: The input encodes W in about log W bits, and W = 2^(log W), so O(nW) is exponential in the input length. Space O(nW) is equally pseudo-polynomial, so space is not what the term refers to.
concept: Pseudo-polynomial: polynomial in numeric values, exponential in their bit length.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: The optimal greedy algorithm for the fractional knapsack problem processes items in which order?
options: Decreasing value
Increasing weight
Decreasing weight
Decreasing value-to-weight ratio
explanation: Taking as much as possible of the highest value-per-unit item first is optimal, by an exchange argument that swaps any lower-ratio volume for higher-ratio volume. Sorting by value alone can fill the knapsack with a heavy item that has a poor ratio.
concept: Fractional knapsack: sort by p/w descending, O(n log n).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Insertion sort is run on A = ⟨5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3⟩. How many element shifts (executions of A[i+1] = A[i]) are performed in total?
explanation: Each shift removes exactly one inversion, and ⟨5,2,4,6,1,3⟩ has 9 inversions, so there are 9 shifts. 12 is the number of key comparisons (each insertion that stops early adds one extra failed comparison), and 15 = C(6,2) would be the reverse-sorted maximum.
concept: Insertion-sort shifts = number of inversions.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: How many inversions does the sequence ⟨4, 1, 3, 2, 6, 5⟩ contain?
explanation: The inversions are (4,1), (4,3), (4,2), (3,2) and (6,5), giving 5. Counting only adjacent out-of-order pairs gives 3 ((4,1), (3,2), (6,5)), which misses non-adjacent inversions such as (4,2).
concept: Inversion: i < j with a_i > a_j.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Solve T(n) = 3T(n/2) + Θ(n).
options: Θ(n log n)
Θ(n)
Θ(n²)
explanation: With a = 3, b = 2, d = 1 we have log₂3 ≈ 1.585 > 1, so the leaves dominate and T(n) = Θ(n^(log₂3)). Θ(n log n) would need a = b^d = 2; it is the merge-sort answer, not this one. This is the Karatsuba recurrence.
concept: a > b^d ⇒ Θ(n^(log_b a)).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Selection sort on A[1..n]: for j = 1 to n−1, find the minimum of A[j..n] and swap it into A[j]. Which loop invariant, holding at the start of iteration j, proves it correct?
options: A[1..j−1] holds the elements originally in A[1..j−1], in sorted order
A[1..j−1] holds the j−1 smallest elements of the array, in sorted order
A[j..n] is sorted in non-decreasing order
A[j] is the smallest element of A[1..n]
explanation: Each iteration moves the minimum of the unsorted suffix into position j, so the prefix always contains the globally smallest j−1 elements in order; at termination (j = n) this gives a sorted array. The 'elements originally in A[1..j−1]' invariant belongs to insertion sort, which never looks beyond the prefix.
concept: Selection-sort invariant: prefix = j−1 smallest, sorted.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
topic: Divide and conquer (merge sort, Karatsuba, max-min)
stem: Karatsuba multiplies x = 2^(n/2)·x_L + x_R and y = 2^(n/2)·y_L + y_R using p₁ = x_L·y_L, p₂ = x_R·y_R and p₃ = (x_L + x_R)(y_L + y_R). Which expression equals x·y?
options: 2ⁿ·p₁ + 2^(n/2)·p₃ + p₂
2ⁿ·p₁ + 2^(n/2)·(p₃ − p₁) + p₂
2ⁿ·p₁ + 2^(n/2)·(p₃ − p₁ − p₂) + p₂
explanation: p₃ − p₁ − p₂ = x_L·y_R + x_R·y_L, the middle term, so only three half-size products are needed. Using p₃ alone double-counts x_L·y_L and x_R·y_R in the middle term.
concept: Gauss trick: middle term = p₃ − p₁ − p₂, giving T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
topic: DFS, edge classification and topological sort
stem: During DFS of a directed graph, edge (u, v) is explored while u is GRAY, and the final timestamps are u: d = 4, f = 5 and v: d = 2, f = 7. What type of edge is (u, v)?
options: Forward edge
Cross edge
Back edge
Tree edge
explanation: The interval [4,5] nests inside [2,7], so u is a descendant of v and the edge points to an ancestor: a back edge, which proves a cycle. A forward edge would need v nested inside u (u.d < v.d), and a cross edge needs disjoint intervals.
concept: Back edge: v.d < u.d < u.f < v.f ⇔ edge to an ancestor.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Kahn's algorithm is run on the DAG with edges 1→3, 2→3, 2→4, 3→5, 4→5, 5→6, always removing the smallest-numbered vertex among those with in-degree 0. What order is produced?
explanation: Initially 1 and 2 have in-degree 0; take 1, then 2, which makes 3 and 4 ready; take 3, then 4, then 5, then 6. The order 1, 2, 4, 3, 5, 6 is also a valid topological order, but it ignores the stated smallest-label tie-break.
concept: Kahn: repeatedly output an in-degree-0 vertex; the tie-break fixes the order.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Run Kruskal's algorithm on the undirected graph with edges A–B 4, A–C 1, B–C 2, B–D 5, C–D 8, C–E 10, D–E 2, D–F 6, E–F 3. What is the weight of the MST?
explanation: Kruskal accepts A–C 1, B–C 2, D–E 2, E–F 3, rejects A–B 4 (cycle A–B–C), then accepts B–D 5 to join the two components: 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 5 = 13. Answering 12 comes from wrongly accepting A–B 4 in place of B–D 5, which leaves the graph disconnected.
concept: Kruskal: sorted edges + union-find; skip cycle-forming edges.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: On the same graph (A–B 4, A–C 1, B–C 2, B–D 5, C–D 8, C–E 10, D–E 2, D–F 6, E–F 3), Prim's algorithm starts at A. In what order are vertices added to the tree?
options: A, C, B, E, D, F
A, C, B, D, E, F
A, B, C, D, E, F
A, C, D, B, E, F
explanation: From {A} the lightest crossing edge is A–C 1; then C–B 2; then the cheapest leaving {A,B,C} is B–D 5; then D–E 2 and E–F 3. E cannot come before D because E is reachable from {A,B,C} only via C–E 10, which is heavier than B–D 5.
concept: Prim grows one tree using the lightest edge leaving it.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Dijkstra's algorithm is run from S on the directed graph S→A 4, S→B 1, B→A 2, A→C 1, B→C 5, C→D 3, B→D 8. What is the final distance to D?
explanation: Extraction order is S(0), B(1), A(3 via B), C(4 via A), D(7 via C). Answering 9 assumes S→B→D 8, which is the first estimate D receives, but it is later improved through C.
concept: Relaxation: d[v] = min(d[v], d[u] + w(u,v)).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Dijkstra's algorithm (which never updates a finalised vertex) is run from S on S→A 2, S→B 5, B→A −4, A→C 1. Which reported distance is wrong?
options: Both A and C (reported 2 and 3; true values 1 and 2)
Only A (C is reported correctly)
Only B
None: there is no negative cycle, so Dijkstra is correct
explanation: A is finalised at 2 and then C at 3 before B (5) is extracted; the edge B→A −4 would give A the value 1, but A is already finalised, so both A and C, which depends on A, stay wrong. 'No negative cycle' is the condition for Bellman–Ford, not for Dijkstra.
concept: One negative edge can break Dijkstra even with no negative cycle.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Coins have denominations {1, 3, 4} (unlimited supply). What are the greedy (largest coin first) coin count and the DP-optimal coin count for amount 10?
options: Greedy 3, optimal 3
Greedy 4, optimal 3
Greedy 4, optimal 2
Greedy 5, optimal 3
explanation: Greedy takes 4 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 4 coins, while the DP finds 3 + 3 + 4 = 3 coins. 'Optimal 2' is impossible because the largest coin is 4 and 2 × 4 = 8 < 10. {1,3,4} is a non-canonical system, so greedy is not safe.
concept: Greedy coin change is optimal only for canonical systems; DP is O(mR).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Unit-time jobs (deadline, profit): J1 (2, 60), J2 (1, 100), J3 (3, 20), J4 (2, 40), J5 (1, 20), J6 (3, 80). The greedy algorithm takes jobs by decreasing profit and puts each in the latest free slot ≤ its deadline. What is the total profit?
explanation: J2 → slot 1, J6 → slot 3, J1 → slot 2; J4, J3 and J5 find no free slot, so the profit is 100 + 80 + 60 = 240. 260 would need a fourth job, but with maximum deadline 3 at most 3 unit jobs can run.
concept: Job sequencing: profit descending, latest free slot ≤ deadline.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Tasks (start, finish): T1 (1,3), T2 (2,5), T3 (4,6), T4 (3,7), T5 (6,8), T6 (7,9), T7 (9,11), T8 (10,12). Using earliest-finish greedy with the strict compatibility rule start > last finish, which tasks are selected?
explanation: T1 (f = 3); T3 starts at 4 > 3 (f = 6); T5 starts at 6, which is not > 6, so it is rejected; T6 starts at 7 > 6 (f = 9); T7 starts at 9, not > 9; T8 starts at 10 > 9. T1, T3, T5, T7 is what the half-open rule start ≥ finish would give, so the stated convention matters.
concept: State the overlap convention (strict > vs ≥) before tracing.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem:
A one-dimensional 0/1 knapsack is coded as:
for each item (c, p):
    for j = c to W:          // upward
        T[j] = max(T[j], p + T[j − c])
With items (c, p) = (2, 3), (3, 4) and W = 4, what does it return, and why?
options: 4, the correct 0/1 optimum
7, because both items are packed
3, because T[j − c] is read before it is written
6, because the upward loop lets item (2, 3) be used twice (unbounded knapsack)
explanation: Going upward, T[2] is already updated to 3 when T[4] reads it, so item (2,3) is counted twice, giving 6; the true 0/1 optimum is 4. The fix is to loop j from W down to c so each T[j − c] still holds the previous row's value.
concept: 1-D 0/1 knapsack must iterate capacity downward.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
topic: Divide and conquer (merge sort, Karatsuba, max-min)
stem: A designer splits n-digit integers into three parts and computes the product with 5 multiplications of n/3-digit numbers plus O(n) extra work (Toom-3). How does this compare with Karatsuba?
options: Θ(n^(log₃5)) ≈ Θ(n^1.465), asymptotically faster than Karatsuba's Θ(n^1.585)
Θ(n^(log₃5)) ≈ Θ(n^1.465), but slower than Karatsuba because log₃5 > log₂3
Θ(n log n), because the combine step is linear
Θ(n²), because 5 > 3 products are needed
explanation: T(n) = 5T(n/3) + O(n) has log₃5 ≈ 1.465 > 1, so T(n) = Θ(n^1.465), which beats log₂3 ≈ 1.585. The number of products alone is misleading: what matters is the exponent log_b a, so 5 products on thirds beat 3 products on halves.
concept: Compare D&C designs by log_b a, not by raw subproblem count.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: T is the MST (weight 13) of the graph A–B 4, A–C 1, B–C 2, B–D 5, C–D 8, C–E 10, D–E 2, D–F 6, E–F 3. A new edge A–F of weight 4 is added. Which O(V) update is correct, and what is the new MST weight?
options: Remove the lightest edge on the A–F path in T (A–C 1) and add A–F: weight 16
Find the A–F path in T, remove its heaviest edge B–D 5 since 4 < 5, and add A–F: weight 12
Keep T, because a new edge can never reduce MST weight: weight 13
Re-run Kruskal from scratch, because local updates are unsafe: weight 13
explanation: The A–F path in T is A–C–B–D–E–F; its heaviest edge is B–D 5 > 4, so by the cycle property B–D leaves and A–F enters, giving 13 − 5 + 4 = 12. Removing the lightest path edge instead raises the weight to 16, the opposite of what the cycle property allows.
concept: Adding edge (x,y): swap it with the heaviest edge on the T-path x–y if lighter.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: A student claims that choosing the shortest task first (then discarding overlaps) maximises the number of compatible tasks. Which instance, with the strict rule start > finish, disproves the claim?
options: Tasks (1,2), (3,4), (5,6): shortest-first takes all three, which is optimal
Tasks (1,5), (6,10), (4,7): shortest-first takes only (4,7), but (1,5) and (6,10) are compatible
Tasks (1,10), (2,3), (4,5): shortest-first takes (2,3), (4,5), which is optimal
Tasks (1,4), (2,5), (3,6): every rule selects one task
explanation: The 3-unit task (4,7) is the shortest, but it overlaps both (1,5) and (6,10), so shortest-first gets 1 task while the optimum is 2. The other instances are cases where shortest-first happens to be optimal, so they cannot disprove the claim.
concept: Disprove a greedy rule with a small counterexample; only earliest-finish is safe.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: The naive recursive Fibonacci algorithm (Fib1) satisfies T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2) + c. What is its growth rate?
options: Linear, Θ(n)
Exponential, Θ(φⁿ) with φ ≈ 1.618
Quadratic, Θ(n²)
Θ(n log n)
explanation: The recurrence mirrors the Fibonacci recurrence itself, so T(n) ≥ F_n, which grows like φⁿ (at least 2^(n/2)). Θ(n) is the iterative Fib2 under unit cost, which avoids recomputing the same subproblems.
concept: Fib1 recomputes subproblems: Θ(φⁿ) time.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Which of the following statements is true?
options: 3n² + 2n + 1 = Θ(n²)
n log n = Ω(n²)
explanation: 3n² ≤ 3n² + 2n + 1 ≤ 6n² for n ≥ 1, so it is Θ(n²) with c = 6 and ε = 3. n log n grows more slowly than n², so it is not Ω(n²); 2^(n+1) = 2·2ⁿ is exponential.
concept: Θ needs both an upper and a lower bound with explicit constants.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Why is selection sort NOT stable?
options: It compares elements with ≥ instead of >
Its long-distance swap can move an element past an equal key, reversing their original order
It uses Θ(n) auxiliary space
It makes Θ(n²) comparisons on every input
explanation: On ⟨2a, 2b, 1⟩ the first pass swaps 1 with 2a, giving ⟨1, 2b, 2a⟩, so the equal keys change order. Θ(n²) comparisons concern speed, not stability, and selection sort is in-place.
concept: Selection sort: in-place, ≤ n−1 swaps, unstable.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
topic: Divide and conquer (merge sort, Karatsuba, max-min)
stem: What is the auxiliary space needed by standard (array-based) merge sort on n elements?
options: Θ(log n) only
Θ(n)
Θ(n log n)
explanation: Merging copies the two halves into temporary arrays L and R, which takes Θ(n) extra space at the top level, reusable across levels. Θ(log n) is just the recursion stack, which ignores the merge buffers.
concept: Merge sort: Θ(n log n) time, Θ(n) extra space, stable.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: For which graphs does BFS from s compute shortest-path distances from s to every reachable vertex?
options: Any graph with non-negative edge weights
Only directed acyclic graphs
Graphs whose edges all have the same (unit) length
Any weighted graph, as long as it is connected
explanation: BFS explores in layers of hop count, and hop count equals path length only when all edges count equally. With general non-negative weights a 2-edge path can be shorter than a 1-edge path, so Dijkstra is needed.
concept: BFS layer i = vertices at hop distance i.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: An undirected graph is bipartite if and only if:
options: It contains no cycle at all
It contains no cycle of odd length
Every vertex has even degree
It is connected and has an even number of vertices
explanation: A cycle must alternate between the two sides, so it has even length; conversely BFS layers give a 2-colouring when no odd cycle exists. 'No cycle at all' is sufficient but not necessary: an even cycle such as a 4-cycle is bipartite.
concept: Bipartite ⇔ no odd cycle; test with BFS 2-colouring.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Which statement is the cut property that proves both Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms correct?
options: The heaviest edge crossing any cut belongs to every MST
The lightest edge of the whole graph is the only safe edge
For any cut that respects the edges chosen so far, a minimum-weight edge crossing the cut can be added safely
Any edge that does not form a cycle can be added safely
explanation: If an MST avoids the light crossing edge e, adding e creates a cycle that crosses the cut at another edge e′ with w(e′) ≥ w(e), and swapping them keeps the tree minimum. 'Any non-cycle edge is safe' ignores weight and would build arbitrary spanning trees.
concept: Cut property: light edge across a respecting cut is safe.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: What is the running time of the Bellman–Ford algorithm on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
options: O((V + E) log V)
O(V + E)
O(VE)
O(E log E)
explanation: Bellman–Ford relaxes all E edges in each of V − 1 passes, plus one extra pass to detect negative cycles, giving O(VE). O((V + E) log V) is Dijkstra with a binary heap, which cannot handle negative edges.
concept: Bellman–Ford: V−1 passes over all edges; detects negative cycles.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: In the subset-sum DP, S[i][j] is true if some subset of the first i elements sums to j. Which recurrence is correct (with the second term used only when aᵢ ≤ j)?
options: S[i][j] = S[i−1][j] AND S[i−1][j − aᵢ]
S[i][j] = S[i][j − aᵢ] OR S[i−1][j]
S[i][j] = aᵢ + S[i−1][j − aᵢ]
S[i][j] = S[i−1][j] OR S[i−1][j − aᵢ]
explanation: Either element i is excluded (S[i−1][j]) or included (S[i−1][j − aᵢ]), and either way suffices, hence OR. Using S[i][j − aᵢ] lets element i be reused, which is the unbounded variant; adding aᵢ mixes arithmetic into a Boolean table.
concept: Subset sum: include/exclude, Boolean OR, O(nX).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: In unit-time job sequencing with deadlines, why is each selected job placed in the LATEST free slot no later than its deadline?
options: It maximises the profit of the current job
It guarantees jobs finish in profit order
It reduces the running time to O(n)
It keeps earlier slots free for later-considered jobs with tighter deadlines
explanation: A job's profit does not depend on which feasible slot it occupies, so placing it as late as possible preserves the most options for jobs whose deadlines are earlier. Placing jobs in the earliest free slot can block a tight-deadline job that would fit otherwise.
concept: Job sequencing: latest free slot ≤ deadline.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Finding both the maximum and the minimum of n elements by processing them in pairs needs how many comparisons (about)?
options: n + ⌈log₂ n⌉ − 2
explanation: Compare each pair once, then the smaller with the current min and the larger with the current max: 3 comparisons per 2 elements. 2n − 2 is the naive method of two separate scans, and n + ⌈log n⌉ − 2 is the count for max and second max.
concept: Max and min together: 3 comparisons per pair.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: With a binary-heap priority queue, Dijkstra's algorithm runs in:
options: O((V + E) log V)
O(V + E)
O(VE)
O(V² log V)
explanation: There are V EXTRACT-MIN and at most E DECREASE-KEY operations, each O(log V). O(V + E) is BFS on unit-weight graphs; O(VE) is Bellman–Ford.
concept: Dijkstra: O((V+E) log V) heap, O(V²) array, O(E + V log V) Fibonacci heap.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Solve T(n) = 4T(n/2) + Θ(n²).
options: Θ(n² log n)
Θ(n²)
Θ(n³)
Θ(n^(log₂4) · n)
explanation: a = 4, b = 2, d = 2 gives log₂4 = 2 = d, the balanced case, so every level does Θ(n²) work over log n levels: Θ(n² log n). Answering Θ(n²) misses the log n factor that comes from the equal-work levels.
concept: a = b^d ⇒ multiply n^d by log n.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Binary search with mid = ⌊(lo + hi)/2⌋ (0-indexed) looks for 34 in ⟨3, 8, 12, 17, 21, 25, 30, 34, 40, 47, 52⟩. Which elements are probed, in order?
explanation: lo = 0, hi = 10 ⇒ mid 5 (25 < 34); lo = 6 ⇒ mid 8 (40 > 34); hi = 7 ⇒ mid 6 (30 < 34); lo = 7 ⇒ mid 7 (34 found). Probing 21 first would use mid = 4, which is not ⌊(0 + 10)/2⌋.
concept: Binary search probes ≤ ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 elements.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: In Merge-and-Count, the sorted halves are A = ⟨1, 3, 7, 8⟩ and B = ⟨2, 4, 5, 6⟩. How many cross inversions are counted during the merge?
explanation: When 2 is output, 3 elements of A remain (3, 7, 8): +3; 4, 5 and 6 each jump ahead of 7 and 8: +2 each, giving 3 + 6 = 9. Adding only 1 per out-of-order comparison (4) misses that a B element is inverted with every remaining A element.
concept: When b_j is output before a_i, add |A| − i + 1.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Selection sort (swap only when the minimum is not already in place) is run on ⟨4, 6, 1, 5, 2, 3⟩. How many swaps are made?
explanation: The passes give ⟨1,6,4,5,2,3⟩, ⟨1,2,4,5,6,3⟩, ⟨1,2,3,5,6,4⟩, ⟨1,2,3,4,6,5⟩, ⟨1,2,3,4,5,6⟩, with a swap in each of the 5 passes. 8 is the inversion count, which governs insertion-sort shifts, not selection-sort swaps.
concept: Selection sort makes at most n − 1 swaps.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: The iterative Fib2 computes F_n with n − 1 additions. Counting bit operations rather than unit-cost word operations, what is its running time?
options: Θ(n), because there are only n − 1 additions
Θ(n log n), because F_n has Θ(log n) bits
Θ(2ⁿ), because F_n grows exponentially
Θ(n²), because F_k has Θ(k) bits and each addition costs time linear in the bit length
explanation: F_n ≈ φⁿ has about 0.694n bits, so the later additions each cost Θ(n) bit operations, giving Θ(n²) in total. Θ(n) holds only in the unit-cost model, which is invalid once numbers exceed a Θ(log n)-bit word.
concept: Unit cost vs bit cost: big numbers make Fib2 quadratic.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
topic: DFS, edge classification and topological sort
stem: DFS on a DAG gives finish times A: 12, B: 7, C: 11, D: 5, E: 9, F: 3. Which topological order does the DFS method produce?
options: F, D, B, E, C, A
A, B, C, D, E, F
A, C, B, E, D, F
A, C, E, B, D, F
explanation: The DFS method lists vertices in decreasing finish time: 12, 11, 9, 7, 5, 3. The order F, D, B, E, C, A sorts by increasing finish time, which reverses every edge.
concept: Topological order = decreasing DFS finish time.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: How many strongly connected components does the directed graph with edges 0→1, 1→2, 2→0, 2→3, 3→4, 4→5, 5→3, 4→6, 6→7 have?
explanation: The SCCs are {0,1,2}, {3,4,5}, {6} and {7}. Answering 2 counts only the cycles and forgets that each vertex not on a cycle (6 and 7) forms its own singleton SCC.
concept: Every vertex belongs to exactly one SCC; singletons count.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: A network wants the spanning tree that maximises total bandwidth. Edges: A–B 3, A–C 6, B–C 4, B–D 2, C–D 7, C–E 5, D–E 1. Running Kruskal in decreasing weight order gives a maximum spanning tree of what weight?
explanation: Taking C–D 7, A–C 6, C–E 5 and B–C 4 (A–B 3 and the rest would close cycles) gives 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 = 22. 10 is the minimum spanning tree weight (D–E 1, B–D 2, A–B 3, B–C 4), the answer to the opposite question.
concept: Maximum spanning tree = Kruskal on decreasing weights.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Dijkstra from A on the directed graph A→B 6, A→C 2, C→B 3, B→D 1, C→D 7, C→E 8, D→E 2. In what order are vertices extracted (finalised)?
options: A, C, B, D, E
A, C, D, B, E
A, B, C, D, E
A, C, B, E, D
explanation: d becomes C 2, B 5 (via C), D 6 (via B), E 8 (via D): extraction A(0), C(2), B(5), D(6), E(8). Extracting D before B assumes D keeps the estimate 9 via C→D and that B stays at 6, but B improves to 5 first.
concept: Dijkstra extracts vertices in non-decreasing final distance.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Bellman–Ford from S on the directed graph S→A 6, S→B 7, A→C 5, A→B 8, A→D −4, B→C −3, B→D 9, C→A −2, D→S 2, D→C 7. What is the final distance to A?
explanation: The best path is S→B (7) → C (4) → A (2), using two negative edges. 6 is the direct edge S→A, the first estimate A receives, before the negative edges propagate. There is no negative cycle, so the value is well defined.
concept: Bellman–Ford handles negative edges; V−1 passes suffice.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: 0/1 knapsack with capacity 6 and items (weight, value): (3, 25), (2, 20), (1, 15), (4, 40), (5, 50). What is the maximum value?
explanation: Weight 1 + 5 gives 15 + 50 = 65, which beats 2 + 4 (60) and 1 + 2 + 3 (60). 75 would need (1,15) + (2,20) + (4,40), whose weight 7 exceeds the capacity.
concept: 0/1 knapsack: K[i][w] = max(K[i−1][w], v_i + K[i−1][w − w_i]).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: What is the minimum number of cuts needed to partition the string "abcbm" so that every piece is a palindrome?
explanation: The partition a | bcb | m uses 2 cuts, and 1 cut is impossible because every two-piece split (a|bcbm, ab|cbm, abc|bm, abcb|m) has a non-palindromic piece. 4 cuts is the trivial bound with all single characters.
concept: Palindrome partitioning: Cuts[i] = min over palindromic s[j..i] of 1 + Cuts[j−1].

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: For A = {3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2}, which target sums are achievable by some subset?
options: Both 9 and 30 are achievable
9 is achievable, 30 is not
30 is achievable, 9 is not
Neither 9 nor 30 is achievable
explanation: 9 = 4 + 5 (or 3 + 4 + 2). Without 34 the total of the remaining elements is 26 < 30, and any subset containing 34 already exceeds 30, so 30 is unreachable.
concept: Subset sum DP decides reachability of every j ≤ X in O(nX).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Fractional knapsack with capacity 30 and items (weight, value): (5, 30), (10, 40), (20, 100), (15, 45). What is the optimal value?
explanation: Ratios are 6, 4, 5, 3: take all of (5,30) and (20,100), then 5/10 of (10,40) for 20, giving 150. 130 comes from taking whole items by value, (20,100) + (5,30), and leaving the remaining capacity unused.
concept: Fractional knapsack: fill by ratio, split only the last item.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Rats at positions {9, 1, 22, 15} must each enter a distinct hole at {30, 3, 12, 10}; each takes 1 minute per unit distance. What is the minimum time by which all rats are inside?
explanation: Sort both: rats 1, 9, 15, 22 and holes 3, 10, 12, 30; paired distances are 2, 1, 3, 8, so the maximum is 8. Any crossing assignment can only raise the maximum (uncrossing lemma). 3 is the largest distance among the first three pairs only.
concept: Rats & holes: sort both, pair i-th to i-th, answer max |r − h|.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: To count the number of distinct shortest s–t paths in an unweighted undirected graph in O(V + E), BFS is extended with cnt[s] = 1. Which update rule is correct when edge (u, v) is scanned from dequeued u?
options: If v is undiscovered: d[v] = d[u] + 1, cnt[v] = cnt[u]; otherwise ignore v
If v is undiscovered: d[v] = d[u] + 1, cnt[v] = cnt[u]; else if d[v] = d[u] + 1: cnt[v] += cnt[u]
For every neighbour v: cnt[v] += cnt[u]
If v is undiscovered: cnt[v] = 1; else if d[v] = d[u] + 1: cnt[v] += 1
explanation: Each shortest path to v ends with an edge from some u in the previous layer, so cnt[v] is the sum of cnt[u] over all such u; BFS dequeues every layer-(d−1) vertex before any layer-d vertex, so the sums are final. Ignoring later discoveries counts only one parent's paths, and adding 1 instead of cnt[u] counts parents rather than paths.
concept: Shortest-path counting: sum counts over previous-layer neighbours.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Each link (u, v) of a network works independently with probability r(u, v) ∈ (0, 1]. To find the most reliable s–t path (maximising the product of r along the path) with Dijkstra, which edge weight should be used?
options: w(u, v) = 1 − r(u, v)
w(u, v) = log r(u, v)
w(u, v) = 1 / r(u, v)
w(u, v) = −log r(u, v)
explanation: Maximising Π r equals minimising Σ −log r, and −log r ≥ 0 for r ≤ 1, so Dijkstra's precondition holds. log r is negative, which breaks Dijkstra; 1 − r and 1/r turn the product into a sum that does not correspond to the product.
concept: Turn products into sums with logs; keep weights non-negative.
source: Scenario type: Cormen et al., ch. 24 exercises

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem:
To count the ways to make amount R from coins C[1..m] where order does NOT matter (multisets), a student writes W[0] = 1 and
for r = 1 to R:
    for each coin c ≤ r: W[r] += W[r − c]
For C = {1, 2, 5}, R = 5, what does this return, and is it correct?
options: It returns 9 and is wrong: it counts ordered sequences; the coin loop must be outermost, giving 4
It returns 4 and is correct
It returns 9 and is correct, since 9 multisets exist
It returns 5 and is wrong because W[0] should be 0
explanation: With amount outermost, 1+2+2 and 2+1+2 are counted separately, giving 9 compositions; looping coins outermost fixes an order of coin types and gives the 4 multisets {5}, {2,2,1}, {2,1,1,1}, {1×5}. Setting W[0] = 0 would make every count 0.
concept: Coin-combinations DP: coin loop outer = combinations; amount loop outer = permutations.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Under the working definition used in algorithm analysis, an algorithm is called efficient when:
options: It runs quickly on the inputs that occur in practice
Its average-case running time is linear
Its worst-case running time is bounded by a polynomial in the input size
It is faster than brute force on at least one input
explanation: The final definition is: there are constants c, d > 0 such that every input of size N takes at most c·N^d steps. 'Runs quickly on real inputs' was rejected because it depends on the platform and on which inputs happen to arrive, and it says nothing about scaling.
concept: Efficient ⇔ polynomial worst-case time.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: T(n) = Ω(f(n)) means:
options: There exist c > 0 and n₀ such that T(n) ≤ c·f(n) for all n ≥ n₀
T(n) ≥ f(n) for at least one n
There exist ε > 0 and n₀ such that T(n) ≥ ε·f(n) for all n ≥ n₀
T(n) and f(n) differ by at most a constant additive term
explanation: Ω is an asymptotic lower bound: beyond some n₀, T is at least a positive constant times f. The '≤ c·f(n)' statement is the definition of O, the upper bound.
concept: Ω = asymptotic lower bound.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: A loop-invariant proof of correctness has three parts. Which list names them?
options: Base case, inductive step, contradiction
Initialisation, maintenance, termination
Divide, conquer, combine
Precondition, recursion, postcondition
explanation: You show the invariant holds before the first iteration, is preserved by each iteration, and at termination (for example j = n + 1) yields the desired result. Divide, conquer and combine are the steps of divide and conquer, not of a correctness proof.
concept: Loop invariant: initialisation, maintenance, termination.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: To which recurrence can the master theorem T(n) = aT(n/b) + O(n^d) NOT be applied directly?
options: T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n²
T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n²
explanation: The master theorem needs a subproblems of equal size n/b; T(n/3) + T(2n/3) has unequal sizes, so a recursion tree is used instead (it gives Θ(n log n)). The other three fit the form with constant a, b and d.
concept: Master theorem: equal-size subproblems, constant a and b, polynomial f(n).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: What is the maximum possible number of inversions in a permutation of n distinct elements, and which permutation achieves it?
options: n − 1, the reverse-sorted permutation
n(n−1)/4, a random permutation
n(n−1)/2, the reverse-sorted permutation
n log n, any permutation produced by merge sort
explanation: In reverse-sorted order every one of the C(n,2) pairs is out of order. n(n−1)/4 is the expected count for a random permutation, not the maximum.
concept: 0 ≤ inversions ≤ C(n,2).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: In Kosaraju's SCC algorithm, the second DFS must be run on:
options: The transpose graph Gᵀ, starting vertices in decreasing order of first-pass finish time
The original graph G, in decreasing order of finish time
The transpose graph Gᵀ, in increasing order of finish time
The original graph G, in increasing order of discovery time
explanation: Starting from the highest finish time in Gᵀ means the DFS cannot leave the source SCC, because the edges leaving that SCC point into it in Gᵀ. Running the second pass on G instead, or in increasing order, lets the DFS spill into other SCCs and merge them.
concept: Kosaraju: DFS(G) → Gᵀ → DFS(Gᵀ) in decreasing f.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: The cycle property of minimum spanning trees states that:
options: The lightest edge on any cycle belongs to no MST
Every MST contains at least one cycle
The heaviest edge of the graph belongs to every MST
The strictly heaviest edge on any cycle belongs to no MST
explanation: If an MST contained the strictly heaviest edge e of a cycle, removing e and adding another edge of that cycle would reconnect the tree at lower weight. The lightest edge on a cycle is often in an MST, so that option reverses the property.
concept: Cycle property justifies Kruskal skipping cycle-forming edges.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: You need shortest-path distances from every vertex TO a single destination t in a directed graph with non-negative weights. What is the standard approach?
options: Run Dijkstra once from t on the original graph
Run Dijkstra from every vertex
Run BFS from t, ignoring the weights
Reverse every edge and run Dijkstra once from t
explanation: A path v ⇝ t in G is a path t ⇝ v in the reversed graph with the same weight, so one Dijkstra run suffices. Running from t on the original graph computes distances from t, which in a directed graph can differ.
concept: Single-destination = single-source on the reversed graph.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: How does memoised (top-down) DP differ from tabulated (bottom-up) DP?
options: Top-down is always asymptotically faster than bottom-up
Bottom-up solves only the subproblems that are actually needed
Top-down does not require optimal substructure
Top-down recurses and caches each subproblem's result; bottom-up fills a table in dependency order without recursion
explanation: Both compute each subproblem once and have the same asymptotic cost; top-down evaluates lazily via recursion with a cache, while bottom-up iterates in an order that makes dependencies available. It is top-down, not bottom-up, that touches only the needed subproblems.
concept: Memoisation vs tabulation: same asymptotics, different evaluation order.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: The greedy-choice property, which greedy algorithms need beyond optimal substructure, states that:
options: Some optimal solution contains the locally best first choice
Every subproblem must be solved and the best combined
The input must be sorted before processing
Each local choice can later be undone if it proves wrong
explanation: If an optimal solution always agrees with the greedy first choice, you can commit to it and solve the single remaining subproblem. Solving every subproblem and combining describes DP; greedy never revisits a choice.
concept: Greedy needs the greedy-choice property plus optimal substructure.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Cats and rats lie on a line in sorted position lists; a cat can catch one rat within distance k. What is the running time of the two-pointer greedy that maximises the number of rats caught?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(n²)
O(nk)
explanation: Each step advances at least one pointer, so the sweep is linear once the positions are sorted (they are given in order). O(n log n) is the rats-and-holes bound, which needs to sort both arrays first.
concept: Cats & rats: two pointers, O(n).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Using a knockout tournament, how many comparisons are needed to find both the largest and the second-largest of n elements?
options: n + ⌈log₂ n⌉ − 2
explanation: The champion needs n − 1 matches; the runner-up must be one of the ⌈log₂ n⌉ players the champion beat, which costs ⌈log₂ n⌉ − 1 more matches. 2n − 3 is the naive two-scan count, and ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2 is for max and min.
concept: Second max is among the players who lost directly to the champion.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Unroll T(n) = T(n−1) + n with T(1) = 1. What is T(n) in closed form and its order?
options: n log n, Θ(n log n)
explanation: T(n) = n + (n−1) + … + 1 = n(n+1)/2, which is Θ(n²). Θ(n log n) would come from treating it as a divide-and-conquer recurrence, but subtracting 1 reduces the size by only one per level, so there are n levels, not log n.
concept: Subtract-type recurrences: unroll; master theorem does not apply.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Order these functions by increasing asymptotic growth: n log n, n^1.5, 2^(log₂ n), (log n)²
options: (log n)², n log n, 2^(log₂ n), n^1.5
(log n)², 2^(log₂ n), n log n, n^1.5
2^(log₂ n), (log n)², n log n, n^1.5
(log n)², 2^(log₂ n), n^1.5, n log n
explanation: 2^(log₂ n) = n, so the order is polylog < n < n log n < n^1.5, because log n = o(n^0.5). Treating 2^(log₂ n) as exponential is the main trap; it simplifies to exactly n.
concept: Simplify exponent-of-log forms: 2^(log₂ n) = n.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem:
A binary search is written as:
while lo < hi:
    mid = ⌊(lo + hi)/2⌋
    if A[mid] < key: lo = mid
    else: hi = mid
What goes wrong?
options: When hi = lo + 1 and A[lo] < key, mid = lo and lo never advances: infinite loop
It returns the wrong index when key is at A[mid]
It reads out of bounds when key is larger than every element
Nothing; it correctly finds the first index with A[i] ≥ key
explanation: With a two-element range, mid = lo; if A[lo] < key the assignment lo = mid changes nothing, so the loop never terminates. Correct forms use lo = mid + 1 so the range strictly shrinks every iteration. It looks like a lower-bound search, which is why 'nothing' is tempting.
concept: Every branch must strictly shrink the search interval.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: The merge step of merge sort combines sorted lists ⟨2, 5, 9, 12⟩ and ⟨1, 3, 4, 15⟩, stopping comparisons when one list is exhausted. How many key comparisons are made?
explanation: Outputs in order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 12 each follow a comparison (7 comparisons); then the first list is exhausted and 15 is copied without comparing. 8 = n₁ + n₂ wrongly counts copying the leftover 15 as a comparison; the maximum possible here is n₁ + n₂ − 1 = 7.
concept: Merging n₁ + n₂ items takes between min(n₁,n₂) and n₁ + n₂ − 1 comparisons.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
topic: Divide and conquer (merge sort, Karatsuba, max-min)
stem: Divide-and-conquer max–min uses C(n) = 2C(n/2) + 2 with C(2) = 1 and C(1) = 0. How many comparisons does it make for n = 16?
explanation: For a power of 2, C(n) = 3n/2 − 2 = 24 − 2 = 22. 30 = 2n − 2 is the naive count of two separate scans.
concept: D&C max–min: 3n/2 − 2 comparisons.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: BFS from vertex 1 in the undirected graph with edges 1–2, 1–3, 2–4, 2–5, 3–6, 4–7, 5–7, 6–7. Which vertices are at distance exactly 2 from vertex 1?
explanation: Layer 1 is {2, 3}; layer 2 is the new neighbours of layer 1: {4, 5, 6}; 7 is first reached from 4 at distance 3. Including 7 confuses the order in which vertices are discovered with their layer.
concept: BFS layers L_i = vertices at hop distance i.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Which of these undirected graphs is NOT bipartite?
explanation: The cycle 2–3–4–5–6–2 has 5 edges, an odd cycle, so no 2-colouring exists. The 4-cycle, the star and the 6-cycle contain only even cycles or none, so they are bipartite.
concept: Look for an odd cycle; BFS finds it as a same-layer edge.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Kruskal's algorithm runs on edges P–Q 2, P–R 3, Q–R 1, Q–S 4, R–S 5, S–T 2, R–T 6 (ties broken in the order listed). Which is the first edge REJECTED?
options: P–R 3
R–S 5
S–T 2
Q–S 4
explanation: Sorted: Q–R 1 ✓, P–Q 2 ✓, S–T 2 ✓, then P–R 3 would close the cycle P–Q–R, so it is the first rejection. R–S 5 is also rejected, but later, after Q–S 4 joins the two components.
concept: Kruskal rejects an edge whose endpoints are already in one component.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: For a dense graph with E = Θ(V²), which Prim implementation gives the best asymptotic running time?
options: Unsorted array of keys: O(V²)
Binary heap: O(E log V)
Sorted edge list with union-find: O(E log E)
Adjacency list with BFS: O(V + E)
explanation: With E = Θ(V²), the binary heap costs O(V² log V), while the array version does V linear-scan extractions for O(V²) in total. Sorting edges is Kruskal, which costs O(V² log V) here; BFS does not compute an MST at all.
concept: Prim: array O(V²) for dense graphs, heap O(E log V) for sparse ones.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Dijkstra from S on the directed graph S→A 7, S→B 2, S→C 9, B→A 3, B→C 6, A→D 4, C→D 1, A→C 1. What is the shortest distance to D?
explanation: The best path is S→B→A→C→D = 2 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 7. 9 is the value through A→D (5 + 4) or S→B→C→D (2 + 6 + 1), both of which are early estimates that the path through A→C improves.
concept: Shortest paths can take more edges; relaxation finds them.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: After V − 1 passes of Bellman–Ford, one extra pass over all edges still relaxes (decreases) some d[v]. What can be concluded?
options: The graph has at least one negative edge, but distances are now correct
More passes are needed because V − 1 is not always enough
Some vertex is unreachable from the source
A negative-weight cycle is reachable from the source
explanation: A simple shortest path has at most V − 1 edges, so if no negative cycle exists, all distances are final after V − 1 passes; any further improvement means some walk keeps getting cheaper, i.e. a reachable negative cycle. Negative edges alone do not cause the V-th pass to relax anything.
concept: Bellman–Ford pass V relaxes ⇔ reachable negative cycle.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Unbounded knapsack (unlimited copies) with capacity 13 and item types (weight, value): (3, 40), (4, 50), (5, 70). What is the maximum value?
explanation: 5 + 5 + 3 = 13 gives 70 + 70 + 40 = 180, which beats 5 + 4 + 4 (170) and 3 + 3 + 3 + 4 (170). 190 would need total weight above 13 (for example 5 + 5 + 4 = 14).
concept: Unbounded knapsack: T[w] = max_i (v_i + T[w − w_i]) on the same table.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Rod cutting with prices p[1..5] = 3, 5, 8, 9, 10. What is the best revenue for a rod of length 5, and how is it obtained?
options: 10, by selling the rod uncut
13, by cutting into lengths 2 and 3
15, by cutting into five pieces of length 1
14, by cutting into lengths 1 and 4
explanation: Length 1 earns 3 per unit, the best rate, so five unit pieces give 15; the DP gives R[k] = 3k for k ≤ 5. 13 (5 + 8) is the tempting 'two pieces' answer, and 10 assumes the longest piece is always best.
concept: Rod cutting must consider all first-cut lengths; the uncut price is just one option.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Cats at {1, 4, 8, 12} and rats at {2, 3, 9, 10, 15}; each cat catches at most one rat within distance k = 1. How many rats does the two-pointer greedy catch?
explanation: Matches: cat 1–rat 2, cat 4–rat 3, cat 8–rat 9; rat 10 is 2 away from cat 12 and rat 15 is 3 away, so no more matches. 4 is the answer for k = 2, where cat 12 can also catch rat 10.
concept: Cats & rats: match the leftmost reachable pair; skip whichever is too far left.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Greedy change-making with coins {1, 5, 10, 25} for amount 63. How many coins are used, and is the result optimal?
options: 5 coins; optimal
6 coins; not optimal, since 5 coins suffice
7 coins; optimal
6 coins (25, 25, 10, 1, 1, 1); optimal
explanation: Greedy takes 2 × 25, 1 × 10 and 3 × 1 = 6 coins, and {1,5,10,25} is a canonical system, so greedy is optimal (the DP also gives 6). A 5-coin answer would need the coins other than quarters to sum to 13 with 3 coins, which is impossible.
concept: Greedy is optimal for canonical systems such as {1,5,10,25}.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: A student replaces the linear scan in insertion sort with binary search to find each key's position and claims the sort is now O(n log n). Evaluate the claim.
options: True: binary search makes each insertion O(log n)
True on arrays, false on linked lists
False: binary search increases comparisons to Θ(n²)
False: comparisons drop to O(n log n), but shifting elements to open the gap still costs Θ(n²) in the worst case
explanation: Binary search finds the slot in O(log j) comparisons, but inserting into an array still moves up to j elements, which on reverse-sorted input is Θ(n²) in total. On a linked list shifting is cheap, but binary search needs random access, so neither structure gives O(n log n).
concept: Count all primitive operations (shifts too), not just comparisons.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: A variant of job sequencing places each job (taken in decreasing profit order) in the EARLIEST free slot instead of the latest. Jobs (deadline, profit): X (2, 50), Y (1, 40). Evaluate the variant.
options: It is optimal, because profit order alone determines which jobs are chosen
It is not optimal: X takes slot 1, so Y cannot be scheduled (profit 50 instead of 90)
It is optimal but slower, because it scans more slots
It is not optimal, but only when two jobs share a deadline
explanation: Earliest-slot puts X in slot 1 and leaves no slot ≤ 1 for Y; latest-slot puts X in slot 2 and Y in slot 1 for 90. The jobs here have different deadlines, so the failure is not limited to shared deadlines.
concept: Slot rule matters: latest free slot preserves feasibility for tight deadlines.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: A constant c > 0 is added to every edge weight of a connected weighted graph. Which statement is correct?
options: Both the MSTs and all shortest paths are unchanged
MSTs can change, but shortest paths are unchanged
Both MSTs and shortest paths can change
Every MST stays an MST, but shortest paths between vertices can change
explanation: Every spanning tree has exactly V − 1 edges, so all of them gain (V − 1)c and their relative order is preserved. Paths have different edge counts, so adding c penalises many-edge paths more: a 2-edge path of weight 2 versus a 1-edge path of weight 3 flips once c = 2.
concept: Monotone weight shifts preserve MSTs but not shortest paths.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Why is worst-case analysis preferred over average-case analysis as the default measure of running time?
options: It is always numerically smaller than the average case
It gives a guarantee for every input and needs no assumption about the input distribution
It is the only measure that ignores constant factors
Average-case running time cannot be expressed in O-notation
explanation: The worst case bounds the time on every input of size n, whereas an average needs a probability distribution, which really describes the input generator rather than the algorithm. The worst case is never smaller than the average, so the first option reverses the relationship.
concept: Worst case = guarantee over all inputs.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: An algorithm performs 5n³ + 100n² log n + 10⁶ steps. What is its tight asymptotic bound?
options: Θ(n³)
Θ(n² log n)
Θ(n³ + n² log n), which cannot be simplified
Θ(10⁶), since the constant term dominates for small n
explanation: Asymptotically the leading term dominates: n² log n = o(n³), and constants vanish, so the bound is Θ(n³). The constant 10⁶ dominates only for small n, and asymptotic notation concerns large n.
concept: Keep the leading term, drop constants and lower-order terms.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: In the merge step of merge sort, ties are resolved with L[i] ≤ R[j] (take from the left list on equality). What does this choice guarantee?
options: An in-place merge with O(1) extra space
Fewer comparisons than using <
Stability: equal keys keep their original relative order
A Θ(n) best case on already-sorted input
explanation: Elements of L came earlier in the input, so taking L first on ties preserves the original order of equal keys. Switching to < still sorts correctly but loses stability; it does not change the space or the Θ(n log n) time.
concept: Merge with ≤ (left wins ties) ⇒ stable merge sort.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
topic: DFS, edge classification and topological sort
stem: A directed graph contains a cycle if and only if a DFS of it finds:
options: A cross edge
A forward edge
A vertex with in-degree 0
A back edge
explanation: A back edge (u, v) points to a GRAY ancestor v, and the tree path v ⇝ u plus (u, v) is a cycle; conversely the first vertex of any cycle that DFS discovers makes the closing edge a back edge. Cross and forward edges point to BLACK vertices and do not imply a cycle.
concept: Directed graph is acyclic ⇔ no back edge.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
topic: Divide and conquer (merge sort, Karatsuba, max-min)
stem: What are the three steps of the divide-and-conquer paradigm?
options: Divide into smaller instances, conquer them recursively, combine the sub-solutions
Sort the input, choose greedily, verify the result
Define states, write a recurrence, fill a table
Initialise, maintain, terminate
explanation: D&C splits the problem into smaller instances of the same problem, solves them recursively, and merges the answers, giving recurrences T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n). States, recurrence and table describe dynamic programming, whose subproblems overlap.
concept: D&C: divide, conquer, combine.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: How does Kahn's topological-sort algorithm reveal that a directed graph has a cycle?
options: It finds a back edge during the traversal
It outputs fewer than V vertices, because at some point no remaining vertex has in-degree 0
Some vertex is output twice
The queue never becomes empty
explanation: Vertices on a cycle never reach in-degree 0, so they are never enqueued, and the algorithm stops with |order| < V. Back edges are how the DFS-based method detects cycles; Kahn's method has no notion of back edges.
concept: Kahn: |output| < V ⇔ cycle.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Which data structure lets Kruskal's algorithm test in near-constant amortised time whether an edge would create a cycle?
options: Min-heap keyed on vertex distance
Adjacency matrix
Union–find (disjoint-set forest)
Stack of visited vertices
explanation: Two endpoints in the same set means the edge closes a cycle; FIND and UNION with path compression cost O(α(V)) amortised. A min-heap keyed on vertices is what Prim and Dijkstra use, not Kruskal's cycle test.
concept: Kruskal = sort edges + union–find.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Prim's MST algorithm and Dijkstra's algorithm have the same structure. What is the key difference in how they update a neighbour v of the extracted vertex u?
options: Prim uses a max-heap; Dijkstra uses a min-heap
Prim sets key[v] = w(u, v); Dijkstra sets d[v] = d[u] + w(u, v)
Prim relaxes only tree edges; Dijkstra relaxes all edges
Prim sets key[v] = d[u] + w(u, v); Dijkstra sets d[v] = w(u, v)
explanation: Prim cares only about the cost of the edge that attaches v to the tree, while Dijkstra cares about the total distance from the source. The last option swaps the two rules, a common mix-up that turns one algorithm into the wrong version of the other.
concept: Prim key = edge weight; Dijkstra key = path length.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Single-source shortest paths on a DAG with arbitrary (possibly negative) edge weights can be computed in which time?
options: O(VE), because negative edges require Bellman–Ford
O((V + E) log V), using Dijkstra
O(V + E), by relaxing edges in topological order
Not at all, because negative edges make shortest paths undefined
explanation: In topological order each vertex's distance is final once all its predecessors are processed, so one relaxation of each edge suffices. Bellman–Ford also works but is slower; negative edges are harmless here because a DAG cannot contain a negative cycle.
concept: DAG shortest paths: topological order + one relaxation per edge.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Which recurrence correctly gives the maximum revenue R[n] for a rod of length n, where a piece of length i sells for p[i]?
options: R[n] = max(p[n], R[n − 1])
R[n] = max over 1 ≤ i ≤ n of (p[i] + R[n − i]), with R[0] = 0
R[n] = max over 1 ≤ i ≤ n of (p[i] · R[n − i])
explanation: Choose the length i of the first piece, then sell the remainder optimally; take the best choice. max(p[n], R[n − 1]) ignores combinations such as 2 + 2, and multiplying prices has no meaning here.
concept: Rod cutting: first-cut choice, O(n²).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Rats and holes on a line: assign each rat to a distinct hole to minimise the maximum distance any rat travels. What is the optimal algorithm?
options: Sort rats and holes, pair the i-th rat with the i-th hole, and return the maximum distance
Send each rat to its nearest free hole, in input order
Sort rats ascending and holes descending, then pair them
Use Dijkstra from every rat
explanation: By the uncrossing lemma, swapping any crossing pair never increases the maximum, so the sorted (non-crossing) pairing is optimal, in O(n log n). The nearest-free-hole rule can leave a later rat with a very distant hole.
concept: Rats & holes: sorted pairing, O(n log n).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Using a precomputed palindrome table Pal[i][j], what is the time complexity of the minimum-cut palindrome partitioning DP on a string of length n?
options: O(n)
O(n³)
O(2ⁿ)
O(n²)
explanation: Filling Pal takes O(n²) and Cuts[i] scans O(i) split points with O(1) table lookups, for O(n²) in total. Checking each substring for being a palindrome on the fly, without the table, would raise this to O(n³).
concept: Palindrome partitioning: Pal table + Cuts, O(n²).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Strassen's matrix multiplication satisfies T(n) = 7T(n/2) + Θ(n²). Solve it.
options: Θ(n² log n)
Θ(n³)
Θ(n²)
explanation: a = 7, b = 2, d = 2: log₂7 ≈ 2.81 > 2, so the leaves dominate and T(n) = Θ(n^(log₂7)). Θ(n³) is the 8-product version, T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n², which Strassen improves on.
concept: Fewer subproblems lower the exponent log_b a.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Letters on line 1 in the order s, p, q, r, t are joined to their capitals on line 2 in the order P, Q, S, T, R. How many pairs of joining lines cross?
explanation: Write each top letter's bottom position in top order: s→3, p→1, q→2, r→5, t→4, giving ⟨3,1,2,5,4⟩, whose inversions are (3,1), (3,2) and (5,4). Two lines cross exactly when their order flips, so crossings equal inversions.
concept: Line crossings reduce to counting inversions.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem:
An insertion-sort inner loop is written (1-indexed) as:
while A[i] > key and i > 0:
    A[i+1] = A[i]; i = i − 1
What is the bug?
options: It should use ≥ instead of > for correctness
When i reaches 0 it reads A[0] before checking i > 0; the test i > 0 must come first
The loop should increment i, not decrement it
There is no bug; the order of conditions does not matter
explanation: With short-circuit evaluation the left condition is evaluated first, so A[0] is accessed out of bounds once the key is smaller than everything in the prefix. Using ≥ would still sort but would break stability; it does not fix the out-of-bounds access.
concept: Guard conditions must precede the accesses they protect.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: In the worst case (key absent), how many key comparisons against A[mid] does binary search make on a sorted array of 100 elements?
explanation: The worst case is ⌊log₂ 100⌋ + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7 probes, since 2⁶ = 64 ≤ 100 < 128. Answering 6 forgets the final probe on a one-element range.
concept: Binary search worst case: ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 probes.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
topic: Divide and conquer (merge sort, Karatsuba, max-min)
stem: Apply Karatsuba's idea to 23 × 47 in base 10 (x_L = 2, x_R = 3, y_L = 4, y_R = 7). What is the middle coefficient p₃ − p₁ − p₂?
explanation: p₁ = 2·4 = 8, p₂ = 3·7 = 21, p₃ = (2+3)(4+7) = 55, so the middle term is 55 − 8 − 21 = 26, and 800 + 260 + 21 = 1081 = 23 × 47. 55 is p₃ itself, used without subtracting p₁ and p₂.
concept: Karatsuba middle term = (x_L+x_R)(y_L+y_R) − x_L·y_L − x_R·y_R.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
topic: DFS, edge classification and topological sort
stem: DFS (alphabetical order of vertices and neighbours) runs on the directed graph a→b, a→c, b→d, c→d, d→a, e→d, e→f. Timestamps come out as a 1/8, b 2/5, d 3/4, c 6/7, e 9/12, f 10/11. What type is the edge c→d?
options: Forward edge
Cross edge
Back edge
Tree edge
explanation: When c→d is explored, d is already BLACK (finished at 4) and d.d = 3 < c.d = 6, so d is not a descendant of c: a cross edge. A forward edge would also target a BLACK vertex, but one with a larger discovery time than the source.
concept: BLACK target: forward if u.d < v.d, cross if u.d > v.d.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Kosaraju's algorithm is run on the directed graph 1→2, 2→3, 3→1, 3→4, 4→5, 5→6, 6→4, 6→7, 7→8, 8→7. Which SCCs does it find?
explanation: Each triangle and the pair 7⇄8 is a cycle, and the edges 3→4 and 6→7 go only forward, so no cycle merges them. Merging {1,2,3} with {4,5,6} would need a path back from 4 to 3, which does not exist.
concept: SCCs: maximal mutually reachable sets; one-way links do not merge them.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: BFS 2-colouring from vertex 1 on the undirected graph with edges 1–2, 1–3, 2–4, 3–4, 3–5, 4–6, 5–6. What is the result?
options: Not bipartite, because 3 and 4 are adjacent
Bipartite with parts {1, 2, 3} and {4, 5, 6}
Not bipartite, because the graph has a cycle
Bipartite with parts {1, 4, 5} and {2, 3, 6}
explanation: The BFS layers are {1}, {2,3}, {4,5}, {6}; even layers {1,4,5} and odd layers {2,3,6}, and no edge joins two vertices of the same layer (3–4 joins layers 1 and 2). Having a cycle is not a problem; only odd cycles prevent 2-colouring.
concept: Even layers vs odd layers give the bipartition.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Prim's algorithm starts at D on the undirected graph A–B 2, A–D 6, B–C 3, B–D 8, B–E 5, C–E 7, D–E 9. Which edges are added, in order?
options: A–B 2, B–C 3, B–E 5, A–D 6
D–A 6, A–B 2, B–E 5, B–C 3
D–A 6, A–B 2, B–C 3, B–E 5
D–B 8, B–A 2, B–C 3, B–E 5
explanation: From {D} the lightest crossing edge is D–A 6 (cheaper than D–B 8 and D–E 9); then A–B 2, then B–C 3 beats B–E 5, then B–E 5. The list A–B, B–C, B–E, A–D is Kruskal's order for the same tree, not Prim's from D.
concept: Prim's edge order depends on the root; the tree weight (16) does not.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: A Dijkstra implementation has no binary heap; it keeps a plain array and, in each of V rounds, scans all vertices to find the unfinalised one with minimum d. What is its running time, and when is it preferable?
options: O(V²); preferable for dense graphs where E = Θ(V²)
O(V²); preferable for sparse graphs
O(E log V); preferable for dense graphs
O(VE); never preferable to a heap
explanation: V scans of O(V) plus O(E) relaxations give O(V² + E) = O(V²). With E = Θ(V²) the heap version costs O(V² log V), so the array wins; on sparse graphs the heap's O(E log V) is better.
concept: Dijkstra: array O(V²) for dense, heap O((V+E) log V) for sparse.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: 0/1 knapsack, capacity 5, items (weight, value): 1: (2, 12), 2: (1, 10), 3: (3, 20), 4: (2, 15). The optimal value is 37. Which items does back-tracking through the table recover?
options: Items 1, 2 and 4
Items 3 and 4
Items 2 and 3
Items 1, 2 and 3
explanation: Weights 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 and values 12 + 10 + 15 = 37. Items 3 and 4 give only 35, and items 1, 2 and 3 weigh 6, over the capacity.
concept: Reconstruct by comparing K[i][w] with K[i−1][w].

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Subset-sum DP for A = ⟨1, 2, 4, 6⟩: S[i][j] is true if some subset of the first i elements sums to j. What is S[3][8], and what is S[4][8]?
options: S[3][8] = true, S[4][8] = true
S[3][8] = false, S[4][8] = true
S[3][8] = false, S[4][8] = false
S[3][8] = true, S[4][8] = false
explanation: The first three elements sum to at most 1 + 2 + 4 = 7, so 8 is unreachable; adding 6 gives S[4][8] = S[3][8] ∨ S[3][2] = false ∨ true = true (6 + 2). A cell can never change from true to false as i grows, which rules out the last option.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Tasks (start, finish): a (1,4), b (3,5), c (0,6), d (5,7), e (3,9), f (5,9), g (6,10), h (8,11), i (8,12), j (2,14), k (12,16). How many tasks does earliest-finish greedy select (strict rule start > last finish)?
explanation: It selects a (f = 4), d (5 > 4, f = 7), h (8 > 7, f = 11) and k (12 > 11), which is 4 tasks. 5 would need another compatible task between these, but every remaining task overlaps one of them.
concept: Earliest-finish greedy is optimal for unweighted task selection.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Unit-time jobs (deadline, profit): A (4, 70), B (100, 60), C (1, 50), D (2, 40), E (1, 30). With slots capped at min(n, d_max), what is the maximum total profit from the greedy schedule?
explanation: Cap the slots at min(5, 100) = 5. A → slot 4, B → slot 5, C → slot 1, D → slot 2, and E (deadline 1) finds slot 1 taken, giving 70 + 60 + 50 + 40 = 220. 250 would include E, which conflicts with C for the single slot ≤ 1.
concept: Large deadlines mean 'no constraint': cap the slot array at n.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: A knockout tournament on 16 players finds the champion. Among how many players must the second-best be searched, and what is the total number of comparisons for max and second max?
options: 15 players; 29 comparisons in total
1 player (the losing finalist); 15 comparisons
8 players; 22 comparisons in total
4 players; 18 comparisons in total
explanation: The champion played ⌈log₂16⌉ = 4 matches, and the true runner-up lost only to the champion, so it is one of those 4; a mini-knockout among them takes 3 comparisons, giving 15 + 3 = 18 = n + ⌈log n⌉ − 2. The losing finalist need not be second best, because the runner-up may have met the champion in an early round.
concept: Second max: n + ⌈log₂ n⌉ − 2 comparisons.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: You must count significant inversions (i < j with a_i > 2·a_j) in O(n log n). Which modification of Sort-and-Count is correct?
options: During the merge, add (remaining in A) whenever a_i > 2·b_j, otherwise output as usual
Sort the array, then count pairs with a_i > 2·a_j by binary search on the original order
Run ordinary inversion counting and divide the result by 2
Before merging the sorted halves, run a separate two-pointer pass that counts, for each b in B, the elements of A greater than 2b; then merge normally
explanation: The merge order compares a with b, but the test compares a with 2b, so the two cannot share one pass; a separate linear pass with a monotone pointer keeps T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). Folding the test into the merge fails: if b_j < a_i ≤ 2·b_j, the merge outputs b_j and moves on, so larger elements of A that do exceed 2·b_j are never counted against it.
concept: When the counting test differs from the merge order, use a separate linear pass.
source: Scenario type: Kleinberg & Tardos, ch. 5 exercises

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: A directed graph is semiconnected if for every pair u, v there is a path u ⇝ v or v ⇝ u. Which O(V + E) test is correct?
options: Check that the component DAG has exactly one source
Run one BFS from any vertex and check that it reaches every vertex
Check that the underlying undirected graph is connected
Compute SCCs, topologically sort the component DAG C₁…C_k, and check that every consecutive pair Cᵢ→Cᵢ₊₁ is joined by an edge
explanation: Semiconnectivity holds exactly when the component DAG has a Hamiltonian path, which in topological order means consecutive components are joined. A single source is not enough: the source can reach two incomparable sinks that cannot reach each other.
concept: Reduce to the SCC DAG; check for a Hamiltonian path in topological order.
source: Scenario type: Cormen et al., ch. 22 exercises

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Weighted interval scheduling: jobs sorted by finish time, p(j) = the last job compatible with j. Which approach is correct?
options: Earliest-finish greedy, because it is optimal for unweighted selection
OPT(j) = max(w_j + OPT(p(j)), OPT(j − 1)), because earliest-finish greedy can drop a heavy job
Pick jobs by decreasing weight and discard overlaps, which is optimal by an exchange argument
OPT(j) = w_j + OPT(j − 1), because every job should be included
explanation: Weights break the greedy argument: a short light job can block one heavy job, so the DP must compare taking j (plus the best compatible prefix) with skipping it. Highest-weight-first also fails: one heavy job can block two compatible jobs whose combined weight is larger.
concept: Weighted intervals need DP; unweighted ones allow greedy.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: A brute-force sort tries every permutation and checks whether it is sorted. What is its worst-case running time?
options: O(n²)
O(2ⁿ)
O(n log n)
O(n · n!)
explanation: There are n! candidate permutations and checking each costs O(n), so the total is O(n·n!); going from n to n + 1 multiplies the work by about n + 1. 2ⁿ underestimates n!, which grows faster than any fixed exponential.
concept: Brute force searches the whole solution space: n! permutations.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Which statement about logarithm bases in asymptotic notation is correct?
options: The base never matters anywhere in asymptotic notation
O(log₂ n) = O(log₁₀ n), but n^(log₂ 3) and n^(log₃ 2) have different orders
O(log₂ n) is strictly larger than O(log₁₀ n)
n^(log₂ 3) = Θ(n^(log₃ 2)) because logs differ only by a constant factor
explanation: Logs of different bases differ by a constant factor, which O absorbs; but in an exponent a constant factor changes the power of n (≈ 1.585 vs ≈ 0.631). That is why the master-theorem exponent log_b a must be computed with the correct base.
concept: Base irrelevant inside O(log n), relevant inside an exponent.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: For a graph with n vertices and m edges, what space does an adjacency list need compared with an adjacency matrix?
options: Adjacency list Θ(n²); adjacency matrix Θ(n + m)
Both need Θ(n + m)
Adjacency list Θ(m log n); adjacency matrix Θ(n²)
Adjacency list Θ(n + m); adjacency matrix Θ(n²)
explanation: Lists store one entry per edge endpoint plus n heads; the matrix stores all n² vertex pairs regardless of how many edges exist. That is why BFS and DFS run in O(n + m) with lists but O(n²) with a matrix.
concept: Sparse graphs: adjacency list; dense graphs or O(1) edge queries: matrix.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Why can't inversion counting in O(n log n) simply list every inversion it finds?
options: Inversions are defined only for pairs of adjacent elements
There can be Θ(n²) inversions, so they must be counted in bulk rather than one at a time
Listing them would need the input to be sorted first
Merge sort cannot detect inversions at all
explanation: A reverse-sorted array has n(n−1)/2 inversions, so any algorithm that touches them individually is Ω(n²). Merge-and-Count adds 'number of elements remaining in A' in O(1) each time an element of B is output first.
concept: Output size can exceed the time budget: count, don't enumerate.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Solve T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1 with T(0) = 0.
options: T(n) = 2n − 1, which is Θ(n)
Θ(n log n), by the master theorem
T(n) = 2ⁿ − 1, which is Θ(2ⁿ)
T(n) = n², which is Θ(n²)
explanation: Unrolling gives 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2^(n−1) = 2ⁿ − 1, the Tower-of-Hanoi recurrence. The master theorem does not apply to subtract-type recurrences, and confusing 2T(n−1) with T(n−1) + 2 gives the linear answer.
concept: Two calls on n − 1 double the work at every level.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Which statement about topological orderings is correct?
options: A directed graph has one if and only if it is acyclic, and it is unique only when the DAG has a Hamiltonian path
Every directed graph has one, but cyclic graphs have several
Every DAG has exactly one topological ordering
A topological ordering lists vertices in increasing DFS discovery time
explanation: A cycle makes it impossible to put every edge forward, and when consecutive vertices are not all joined by edges they can be swapped, giving another valid order. Ordering by discovery time fails, for example, when a vertex discovered later has an edge into one discovered earlier.
concept: Topological order exists ⇔ DAG; often not unique.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: When is the minimum spanning tree of a connected weighted graph guaranteed to be unique?
options: When the graph has no cycles of equal weight
Always; the MST is always unique
When all edge weights are distinct
When the graph is dense
explanation: With distinct weights every cut has a unique light edge, so there is only one MST. With ties several trees can share the minimum weight; the MST weight is always unique but the tree need not be.
concept: Distinct weights ⇒ unique MST; MST weight is always unique.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: The optimal-substructure property of shortest paths states that:
options: Every sub-path of a shortest path is itself a shortest path between its endpoints
Every shortest path uses the minimum-weight edge of the graph
The shortest path from s to t is part of the MST
Combining shortest paths s ⇝ u and u ⇝ t always gives a shortest path s ⇝ t
explanation: If a sub-path could be shortened, splicing in the shorter piece would shorten the whole path (cut-and-paste). The last option is the converse, which fails whenever u is not on a shortest s–t path.
concept: Sub-paths of shortest paths are shortest.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Why does Bellman–Ford use exactly V − 1 relaxation passes?
options: With no negative cycle, some shortest path is simple and so has at most V − 1 edges; pass k fixes paths of k edges
Each pass finalises exactly one vertex, as in Dijkstra
V − 1 is the number of edges in a spanning tree, which the algorithm builds
It is a heuristic; more passes may sometimes be needed without negative cycles
explanation: After pass k, every vertex whose shortest path has at most k edges has its correct distance, and simple paths have at most V − 1 edges. Bellman–Ford does not finalise one vertex per pass; that is Dijkstra's behaviour.
concept: Bellman–Ford correctness: simple shortest path ≤ V − 1 edges.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: In the 2-D table, what distinguishes the 0/1 knapsack recurrence from the unbounded one in the 'include item i' term?
options: 0/1 reads row i; unbounded reads row i − 1
0/1 uses min; unbounded uses max
0/1 reads row i − 1 (item used at most once); unbounded reads the same row i (item reusable)
There is no difference; only the initialisation changes
explanation: Reading K[i−1][w − wᵢ] means the remaining capacity is filled without item i, so it is used at most once; reading K[i][w − wᵢ] allows item i again. Swapping the rows is exactly the bug that turns one variant into the other.
concept: Same-row lookup ⇒ unlimited reuse.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Why does the value-to-weight ratio greedy, optimal for fractional knapsack, fail for 0/1 knapsack?
options: Its exchange argument swaps a small fraction δ of one item for another, which is impossible when items are indivisible
Ratios cannot be computed when weights are integers
0/1 knapsack requires items sorted by weight instead
The greedy runs out of time on 0/1 instances
explanation: With divisible items any lower-ratio volume can be replaced by higher-ratio volume, but whole items may leave unusable capacity; for example capacity 50 with (10,60), (20,100), (30,120) gives greedy 160 but optimum 220. Sorting by weight fails too, so no simple sort rescues 0/1.
concept: Fractional: greedy; 0/1: DP.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Which proof technique shows that earliest-finish greedy is optimal for task selection?
options: Greedy stays ahead: by induction the r-th greedy task finishes no later than the r-th task of any optimal solution
The cut property
Loop invariant on a sorted prefix
Master theorem
explanation: If f(g_r) ≤ f(o_r) for every r, an optimal solution with more tasks would have a task greedy could still have taken, which is a contradiction. The cut property proves MST algorithms, not interval scheduling.
concept: Task selection: greedy stays ahead.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Insertion sort is run on ⟨7, 3, 5, 1, 9, 2⟩. What does the array look like after the outer loop has inserted the first four elements (i.e. after the iteration for j = 4, 1-indexed)?
explanation: After j = 2: ⟨3,7,5,…⟩; after j = 3: ⟨3,5,7,…⟩; after j = 4 the key 1 moves to the front: ⟨1,3,5,7,9,2⟩. ⟨3,5,7,1,9,2⟩ is the state one iteration earlier, before 1 is inserted.
concept: Invariant: A[1..j] is the original prefix, sorted.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n²).
options: Θ(n² log n)
Θ(n log n)
Θ(n³)
Θ(n²)
explanation: a = 2, b = 2, d = 2: log₂2 = 1 < 2, so the root dominates, and the level sums n², n²/2, n²/4, … form a decreasing geometric series. Adding a log n factor applies only in the balanced case a = b^d.
concept: a < b^d ⇒ Θ(n^d).

subject: Algorithm Analysis
topic: Divide and conquer (merge sort, Karatsuba, max-min)
stem: Bottom-up merge sort is applied to ⟨38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10, 15⟩. What are the two sorted runs just before the final merge?
explanation: Pairs become ⟨27,38⟩ ⟨3,43⟩ ⟨9,82⟩ ⟨10,15⟩, and these merge into the two sorted halves of the original positions. ⟨3,9,10,15⟩ / ⟨27,38,43,82⟩ splits the final sorted output by value, which is not how merge sort divides the array.
concept: Merge sort splits by position, not by value.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
stem: Two users rank six films. Listed in user 1's order, user 2's ranks are ⟨6, 2, 8, 4, 1, 7⟩. How many film pairs do the two users order differently (inversions)?
explanation: Pairs: 6 is before 2, 4 and 1 (3); 2 before 1 (1); 8 before 4, 1 and 7 (3); 4 before 1 (1), so the total is 8. 15 = C(6,2) would mean complete disagreement.
concept: Ranking disagreement = number of inversions.

subject: Algorithm Analysis
